name: Mass gainer powders

card.summary: Calorie-dense carb-and-protein shake powders for lifters who struggle to eat enough; they add calories, and the evidence is about overall energy intake rather than the powder itself.
card.note: Some products have been linked to contamination with undeclared steroids; one case report links a steroid-containing mass gainer to pancreatitis.

quick.overview:
A mass gainer is a powdered supplement mixed into a shake that delivers a large number of calories per serving, usually from carbohydrate, protein and fat. It is aimed at people trying to gain body weight and muscle who find it hard to eat enough food.

According to Grokipedia, typical servings supply 500 to 1,500 calories with a protein-to-carbohydrate ratio of around 1:2 or more [1]. Looksmaxxing forum users disagree about whether they are useful or whole food is preferable [2].
quick.mechanism: The mechanism is a caloric surplus: eating more energy than is used is needed to gain weight, and resistance training directs part of the gain toward muscle. A powder is a convenient, energy-dense way to add calories, often built on whey and maltodextrin [1]. A registered overfeeding-plus-resistance-training trial has examined body composition changes under surplus feeding, but results are not described in the registration [3].
quick.risks: Dietary supplements in the US are regulated as foods and manufacturers confirm product safety themselves [4]. A review of FDA data found muscle-building products among those contaminated with undeclared anabolic steroids [4], and a 2025 case report describes pancreatitis with panniculitis in a patient who took a weight-gain supplement thought to contain anabolic steroids [5]. Users also report digestive complaints and acne in forums [2].

lead: A mass gainer, or weight gainer, is a high-calorie powder supplement designed to help people gain weight and muscle by supplying a large amount of energy, mostly from carbohydrate with moderate protein and some fat, in a drinkable form [1].

Mass gainers are discussed in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing communities by "hardgainers" and by people bulking. Some lifters regard them as a convenient way to hit calorie targets; others in the same forums argue that whole foods or plain protein are preferable [2].

Evidence specific to mass gainers as a product category is limited. The underlying principle, that weight gain requires a caloric surplus, is general nutrition; published case reports describe harms from products adulterated with steroids [5].
infobox: Carbohydrate (often maltodextrin), whey protein, fats, vitamins and minerals [1]

paras: Grokipedia describes mass gainers as combining whey protein concentrate, rapidly absorbed carbohydrate such as maltodextrin, and fats, sometimes with added vitamins, minerals, amino acids and digestive enzymes [1]. They differ from whey isolate products, which focus on protein with fewer calories [1].

Grokipedia traces calorie-dense muscle-building products to late 19th-century items such as Bovril and Plasmon, and says homemade high-calorie shakes were promoted to bodybuilders in the 1970s and 1980s, with commercial products from firms such as Weider and Optimum Nutrition following [1]. The article states online retail in the 2000s widened availability. These historical claims come from an AI-generated encyclopedia and have not been independently verified here.

In the US, DSHEA (1994) treats supplements as foods; manufacturers need no pre-approval and the FDA generally acts after a problem arises [4]. A study of supplements sold from 2007 to 2016 found 776 products with undeclared pharmaceuticals, and muscle-building products were contaminated with anabolic steroids [4]. Consumer Reports has reported heavy metals in several protein powders, and "protein spiking" allegations have been reported, which some companies disputed [4].

A 2025 case report in the Pakistan Journal of Medical Sciences describes life-threatening pancreatitis with panniculitis associated with a weight-gain supplement; the report notes that mass gainers containing anabolic steroids have been linked in the literature to acute pancreatitis [5].

No clinical trials of mass gainer powders as a product have been found. A registered trial of overfeeding combined with resistance training in 32 participants (started 2019) examined body composition changes under a calorie surplus, and is about overfeeding generally rather than a commercial gainer [3]. Related research on whey protein reports moderate evidence that whey is a safe and effective add-on to training, though reviews disagree on whether high protein intakes meaningfully raise muscle mass [4].

timeline.event: DSHEA places dietary supplements in the US under food-style regulation [4].
Case report links a weight-gain supplement to pancreatitis with panniculitis [5].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, mass gainers come up in discussions of bulking and supplements, with users split on whether they are useful [2].

claims.claim: Mass gainers harm gut health and may cause acne, so whole food is better.
claims.believers: One looksmax.org user who stopped using mass gainers, protein powder and creatine said he suspected the ingredients were poorly absorbed, disrupted his gut and may have contributed to his acne [2].
claims.experts: No published study cited here has tested mass gainer powders for acne or gut effects; the available documented harms involve adulterated products [4][5].

claims.claim: Carbs and calories matter more than large amounts of protein for gaining.
claims.believers: Some forum replies argue that a moderate protein intake is enough and extra calories should come from carbohydrate, while others in the thread disagreed strongly [2].
claims.experts: Recommended protein intakes differ (0.8 g/kg/day RDA versus about 1.2 to 1.8 g/kg/day suggested for athletes), and reviews disagree about benefits of high protein intake [4].
